runs.answer:
# The Clockmaker's Last Apprentice

Wind up the mainspring, feel the deep strain
That runs within each silver and copper vein;
The years have worn the wheels and tiny springs,
Yet still the steady, patient motion clings.

Tick by tick, the brass escapement swings,
Releasing each controlled and measured thing.
I taught thee how the balance and the wheel
Divide the hours into equal spell.

Rust creeps across each surface worn and bare,
In every lever made of brass or steel;
Thou cannot bar the slow decline of gear,
Nor summon back the strength that years stole.

Chime though it does, the bell grows weak and thin,
Its voice grows faint, its power wearing slight;
Some losses cannot be mended, that's the way,
Only endured and kept through dark and day.

Stop when the final wheel at last halts still,
When springs unwind and gears fulfill their will;
Will thou preserve what cannot be made whole?
Is keeping what we have our only role?

runs.answer:
# The Clockmaker's Last Apprentice

Wind the mainspring tight and hold it fast,
As I have done from youth unto this day.
Each gear must catch and turn as I have cast,
And drive the works along their appointed way.

Tick by tick the pendulum swings,
A measure thou must learn to hear.
No clock can stop the flow it brings,
No matter how many wheels appear.

Rust will come to every iron part,
Though oil may stay it for a little span.
Some things decay and that is nature's art,
Beyond thy skill or mine to understand.

Chime by chime the hours pass away,
Each marking off a moment gone for good.
We cannot mend the years or make them play,
But we can wind the clock as you should.

Stop the clock at last when I am gone,
And take my tools to keep the bench supplied.
Thou must remember lessons I have drawn,
To guard, not fix, what we have tried?

runs.answer:
# The Clockmaker's Last Apprentice

Wind the mainspring slow and steady true,
As I taught to thee this patient view.
Some gears grind, some springs unwind,
But steady hands and faithful hearts abide.

Tick by tick, the silent hours pass,
Too much weight, too heavy, on the mass
That presses on thee, still so fair;
Breathe within the measured, cool, calm air.

Rust will come to every tiny tooth,
Though we scrub it, scour, and smooth.
What is lost can never be restored,
But we guard what still remains, what is spared.

Chime by chime, the bronze bell declares
That the work is done, my cares.
Take the bench, the tools, the trade,
And the deep wisdom I have made.

Stop and hear the silence now,
As the final pendulum bows.
Will thou keep the flame alight
When old Ben has now gone from sight?

runs.answer:
# The Clockmaker's Last Apprentice

Wind the mainspring, boy, with patient hand,
For the work must be complete and good.
Every wound is small command,
That the mechanism stay its blood.

Tick by tick the moments pass away,
One by one, like sand through fingers poured.
Thou wilt learn to count them day by day,
But never know what they have cost or stored.

Rust will find each iron part,
Creeping in where oil could not go.
What thou seekest cannot restart;
Some must simply be preserved, I know.

Chime will fade to stillness at the end,
But the frame remains for someone dear.
Keep the case, the face, each dial, friend,
Even when the hands refuse to steer.

Stop me when the final work is past,
For my hands are weary and worn through.
Tell me, lad, when I'm laid in the grass,
Will thou keep what I have taught to do?

runs.answer:
# The Clockmaker's Last Apprentice

Wind the mainspring tight, dear lad, my faithful boy,
And heed the words I bid you hear today:
Though I depart, the craft shall stand
As long as thou art drawing near.

Tick goes the wheel, a ceaseless sound,
Like breath of some small living thing;
No matter what thou see'st around
May lose or fade, it still can ring.

Rust creeps along my iron case,
As years always wear down the brass and steel inside;
Some gears may soon break in their embrace,
Beyond what any wrench can heal or guide.

Chime will the bell at hours due,
Though I shall not remain to hear it sound,
What once was bright, now faded too,
Still marks the path for thee to walk around.

Stop now my hand; the work is done,
And I must lay my tools at last.
Some things once broken, one by one,
Can never be made whole; is that past?

runs.answer:
# The Clockmaker's Last Apprentice
Wind, soft and slow, across my hair,
Thee must learn my patient care.
Some broken parts no oil can make less sore,
Only gently tend them at the door.

Tick by tick my hands grow weak,
Thee must keep my counsel, gentle and meek.
A cracked spring will not be sound,
Only kept in still and quiet bound.

Rust shall claim the gears I have known,
Thee, dear boy, my counsel is your own.
What has worn beyond its final grace,
May be kept in tender place.

Chime by chime the quiet evening nears,
Thee must wipe the soft and silent tears.
Some things fail beyond all repair,
Yet their keeping still fills the air.

Stop thy tools at the bench, my last advice:
Hold no part in vain device.
When the hour has quite gone away,
Can kept love last another day?

runs.answer:
# The Clockmaker's Last Apprentice
Wind will fold around thee waiting hand,
When I can no more the bench command.
Hold the broken springs as made,
Some wounds are kept, but gently swayed.

Tick by tick, thou hear the slow decay,
Of gears that will not come back today.
Keep hollows near thy breast, I pray,
For lost things live where they stay.

Rust may climb where polish used to gleam,
And silver lose its old and steady beam.
Yet thou canst keep fragments, near and dear,
Where patient hands keep them through the year.

Chime will not rise from the cracked bell's tongue,
Nor spring restore the hush of the young.
Keep the broken note, as I said,
For what is kept may softly spread.

Stop, dear boy, when the day grows dim,
And lay down the oil and thin rim.
What cannot be mended, keep it near,
Shall I ask if mending is here?

runs.answer:
# The Clockmaker's Last Apprentice
Wind my lad, the dust on thy bench doth fall,
I have loved thy care through each winter's call.
I have taught thee to keep the hours at bay,
Till this last day the light doth play.

Tick by tick, the little silver tick
Hath worn its path, and no hand makes it quick.
Yet keep what fades: the wound we cannot fix
Doth ask for tenderness, not proud tricks.

Rust creeps in where polish used to dwell,
And sets a slow and sorrowful spell.
To thee I say, when springs are past repair,
We keep the shape, and let the ache be there.

Chime boy, when voices fail,
The kept thing speaks; none prevail.
We do not mend the thread;
We keep the loss, and softly tread.

Stop my lad, when mending doth cease,
What remains to bless our peace?
Keep it near, let it be;
Shall I trust thee with me?
